name: Pueblo of Isleta grant, confirmed by the Act of December 22, 1858 and patented in 1864
citation: Act of December 22, 1858, ch. 5, 11 Stat. 374 (claim Q, Pueblo of Isleta)
promises: This was not a cession. Congress confirmed the Pueblo of Isleta's land claim, as reported favorably by the Surveyor General of New Mexico, and directed that a patent issue for it (Act of December 22, 1858). Royce lists it as confirmed in 1858 and patented in 1864 for 110,080.31 acres.
The Act said the confirmation was only a relinquishment of the United States' own title and claim and did not affect any adverse valid rights.

Later law, not part of the grant: in the Pueblo Lands Act of 1924 the United States, in its sovereign capacity as guardian of the Pueblo Indians, undertook to quiet title to Pueblo lands and made itself liable for losses it could have prevented by seasonable prosecution.
landTaken: None documented inside this grant. The Pueblo Lands Board's Isleta losses that the Indian Claims Commission describes lie outside it: the 14,710.85-acre Peralta tract in the Lo de Padilla Grant (patented to Isleta in 1908) and fifteen tracts of 59.848 acres in the Gutierrez and Sedillo grants.
compensation: The Act of May 31, 1933 authorized $47,751.31 for Isleta in addition to the Pueblo Lands Board's awards, and $6,624.45 for non-Indian claimants within the pueblo of Isleta whose claims the Board did not sustain. The Indian Claims Commission records (Docket 211, Findings 17 to 21) that this sum included $29,421.70 for the 14,710.85-acre Peralta tract in the Lo de Padilla Grant at $2 an acre, which Isleta received; the Board had made no award for that tract but awarded $2 an acre for two small tracts in the same area. What land the rest of the 1933 sum covered was not found; the scan of the House committee's figure for it is unreadable. The Indian Claims Commission held in other pueblos' cases that this Pueblo Lands Act compensation was not a Fifth Amendment taking, because Congress as trustee paid full market value (Taos, 1971; San Ildefonso and others, 1976).
today: The grant remains Isleta land; the Commission's findings record a supplemental patent of October 7, 1933 for land erroneously omitted from the 1864 survey. In 1959 the Indian Claims Commission dismissed Isleta's Docket 211 claims for the Peralta tract and the Bosque de los Pinos tract, both outside this grant, finding the Peralta settlement fairly negotiated before the Pueblo Lands Board and the Bosque tract never Isleta's; the Court of Claims affirmed (152 Ct. Cl. 866, March 10, 1961) and the Supreme Court denied certiorari (368 U.S. 822). Those were rulings against the nation. In 1949 the United States put three tracts of 17,492 acres, including most of the Peralta tract, in trust for Isleta (63 Stat. 604, as recorded by the Commission).

openQuestions: The date 1886-10-01 is the heading of Royce's schedule section, not an event; this record is Isleta's confirmed grant, land kept rather than ceded. treaties.json names it a "cession".
The Commission's 1959 findings give the supplemental patent of October 7, 1933 an acreage that the scan renders unclearly (about 20,000 acres); it is left out of the record.
The Pueblo of Isleta's own account of its land losses was not found on isletapueblo.com.
treaties.json links a University of Georgia PDF (677r.pdf) that was not opened.

Audit 2026-11-08: downgraded from broken to no-breach-found. Both breaches rested on the Act of May 31, 1933 (48 Stat. 108). Opened: section 1 does say 'in payment of the liability of the United States to the said pueblos as declared by the Act of June 7, 1924', and section 2 names 'pueblo of Isleta, $47,751.31'. But the Act gives one sum per pueblo and does not say where the land lay, and Isleta held other grants besides this one. ICC Docket 211, Findings 16 to 21 (OSU id 194), summarising the Board's two Isleta reports of August 1928 and the 1932 and 1933 congressional reports, place the losses it describes outside this grant: $29,421.70 of the 1933 sum was for the Peralta tract in the Lo de Padilla Grant, and the Board's other awards it mentions were for tracts in the Lo de Padilla and Gutierrez-Sedillo grants. No source opened ties any loss to the 1858/1864 Isleta grant (Royce's area), so the 1933 Act cannot carry a breach on this record. If the Board's Report No. 2 on Isleta shows extinguished claims inside the 1864 grant, the breach could be restored.

Audit 2026-11-08: lead: the Peralta loss belongs to the Lo de Padilla Grant, which has no Royce record; it could be an extra- record, though the Commission held that settlement fair and Congress paid for it.

Audit 2026-11-08: the day of the Board's Isleta reports is unclear in the scan ('August 37, 1928'); a search summary of J. J. Bowden's history gives August 17, 1928, but that page did not load. Left as August 1928.

Audit 2026-11-08: Pueblo ruling (coordinator, 2026-11-08): the Act of May 31, 1933 (48 Stat. 108) is not a finding or a government admission. It has no findings or preamble; section 2 pays sums 'in addition to' the Board's awards, by pueblo, not by grant, and its 'liability of the United States ... as declared by the Act of June 7, 1924' wording covers every pueblo it names. The Indian Claims Commission held there was no Fifth Amendment taking because Congress, as trustee, paid full market value (Pueblo of Taos, Docket 357-A, 24 Ind. Cl. Comm. 414, February 10, 1971; San Ildefonso et al., Docket 354, 39 Ind. Cl. Comm. 34, September 16, 1976, both opened). Applied here: the 1933 sums are recorded only as compensation, and no other source ties a loss inside this grant to a Board finding or a taking holding, so the record is no-breach-found.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for Pueblo, Isleta, Isleta grant; Pueblo de Isleta, 152 and 155 Ct. Cl. (1961), are the already-recorded Docket 211 appeal; the ICC aboriginal-title decisions found expressly exclude the confirmed grants (e.g. 30 Ind. Cl.
